newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EFTA signs trade pact with Morocco, eyes others.
newsitem.headline: EFTA signs trade pact with Morocco, eyes others.

text.p: The four-nation European Free Trade Association (EFTA) on Thursday signed a pact with Morocco to create a free trade area by the year 2010, as well as declarations of co-operation with Jordan and Lebanon.

A communique from EFTA -- which links Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein -- said the 37-year-old grouping was also well advanced in talks on a free trade pact with Tunisia and would begin negotiations with Cyprus shortly.

It also confirmed that EFTA, which accounts for some three per cent of world trade, was considering expanding its horizons beyond Europe and the Mediterranean to forge links with groupings in Asia and Latin America.

The communique was issued following a bi-annual meeting of the EFTA Council, attended by trade ministers of the four -- all of whom except Switzerland are linked to the European Union in the European Economic Area (EEA).

EFTA said the progressive expansion of its network of agreements with Middle Eastern and North African countries would make it possible for companies based in its member states to take part in the EU project for a Mediterranean free trade zone.

The Geneva-headquartered grouping -- which once included six of the current 15 members of the EU -- already has free trade accords with Israel and Turkey as well as with 10 ex-Soviet or ex-communist European states from Estonia to Bulgaria.
It is also working towards an agreement with Egypt.

Despite the relatively small geographic size and population of its members, EFTA officials argue that their combined gross domestic product of some $470 billion and foreign trade worth $240 billion give them significant weight in the world economy.

Although EFTA's 11 million people are equal to just three per cent of the population of the EU, their foreign trade is equal to one sixth of that of the Union -- which is itself the world's leading trading power.

Under the agreement with Morocco, the four EFTA countries will remove all tariffs and quotas on imported industrial products, processed agricultural goods, fish and other marine products as soon as it is ratified by national legislatures.

Morocco will abolish its own duties on EFTA products over a transition period of 12 years, and will be allowed to introduce temporary measures to protect infant industries and sectors of its national economy undergoing liberalisation.
But, like all EFTA free trade accords, the agreement does not cover farm produce, arrangements for which are negotiated individually by the four member countries with trading partners.
The communique said the ministers planned in the future "to discuss the establishment of links with other countries and regional groupings" further afield than the immediate vicinity of Europe.

EFTA Secretary-General Kjartan Johannsson of Iceland recently indicated initialed contacts had already been made with the seven-member Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and Latin America's four-nation Mercosur, but they were not specified in the communique.
